buyBody: A blade tells you the truth about every putt you hit, which is exactly why better putters keep going back to them. This one is milled from a single block of 431 stainless and heavy for its size, so there is nothing inside it to ring and nothing in your hands to take over on a short one. Right hand, sixty days, and out of stock at the moment.

clubHeadline: A smaller head tells you more. Roll one pure and you'll know it.
clubParas: A blade does less for you than a mallet and asks more in return, which is exactly why better putters keep going back to them. It is milled from a single block of 431 stainless, so there is nothing inside it to ring or buzz and the feedback comes back honest rather than harsh: you feel where on the face you hit it, every time. At 385 grams it is heavy for a blade, and that weight is what keeps it planted through a four-footer when the hands want to help.

clubSpecs.v: Blade putter, CNC-milled from a single block of 431 stainless.
Muted and solid at impact. No ring, no ping, no buzz through the hands, and honest feedback on the ones you miss.
One-piece 431 stainless head, milled face, 3.5° of loft and 385 g at 35 inches. Gold finish, Lucky rubber grip.
Players who release the head through the stroke and would rather know about a miss than have it covered up.

videoBrief: 16:9 product film, 40–60s. Down-the-line showing the arc the head wants to travel on, then the face at impact in slow motion. A blade's argument is feel, which is the hardest thing to film. Lean on sound.

look.photo: Bold, full-bleed, portrait. Blade head at address on the green, low sun along the top line. Shot from the golfer's eyeline so the small head reads as small. That is the appeal.
look.headline: Less club, more information
paras: A blade is the smallest thing you will look down at all round, and every miss tells you about itself. That is either the reason to play one or the reason not to.
In gold, at 385 grams, it is also the least apologetic putter we make.
If you would rather the head covered the miss than reported it, the Tracer Mallet is the other one.
look.aside: Everyone else is carrying the same putter with someone else's name on it. It's better to be lucky.

helpPick.headline: Both suit an arc. The question is feel or forgiveness.
helpPick.sub: This is the only question worth asking about a putter and the usual answer (mallets for straight strokes, blades for arcs) does not apply here. Both Tracers are built for a stroke with a natural arc. What separates them is how much the head helps you on the ones you miss, and how much it tells you about them.

options.name: Tracer Blade
options.body: For players who release the head through the stroke. Twenty grams heavier and far less forgiving, which is the trade: a blade tells you exactly where on the face you hit it.

options.name: Tracer Mallet
options.body: Slight toe hang from a plumber neck, so it works with the arc you already have. Perimeter weighting keeps an off-center strike on line. You give up some feedback to get that.

helpPick.note: The blade is out of stock and right hand only when it returns. If you want the feedback rather than the forgiveness, that is worth waiting for.

clubGrinds.v: It is the smallest thing you will look down at all round and the most honest. A blade will not straighten out a strike you missed, and that is the trade you are making: it tells you exactly what you did instead. For players who release the head through the stroke.

clubGrinds.k: The grip: nothing in the way
clubGrinds.v: The stock Lucky rubber grip, not the oversized 3.0 that ships on the mallet. That pairing is deliberate. An arcing stroke wants to feel the club, and a fat grip is designed to take exactly that away.
